title: The evolving liquidity landscape − speech by Victoria Saporta
summary: Bank of England Executive Director Victoria Saporta discussed how central bank balance sheet normalization, higher global government bond issuance, and expanding NBFI presence are creating a new liquidity environment with increased demand for funding through government bond repo markets. Sterling reserves have decreased by approximately £322bn since QT began, with the Bank's STR and ILTR facilities now supplying £152bn of reserves versus £12bn in January 2024. The estimated Preferred Minimum Range of Reserves (PMRR) is £375-540bn, and the Bank expects to reach the upper range without further facility growth by late next year.
key_points: Central bank balance sheets are normalizing across major economies, shifting from years of plentiful reserves to falling but still ample supply
Sterling reserves have decreased by approximately £322bn through Quantitative Tightening and TFSME repayments since February 2022
Bank of England's Short-Term Repo (STR) and Indexed Long-Term Repo (ILTR) facilities now supply £152bn of reserves, up from £12bn in January 2024
The Preferred Minimum Range of Reserves (PMRR) is estimated at £375-540bn based on counterparty surveys; without further facility growth, upper range expected by end of next year
ILTR minimum spread for Level A collateral increasing from 0 to 3 basis points to balance incentives between STR and ILTR facilities

A recent liquidity bump saw overnight General Collateral gilt repo rates rise to over 30 basis points above Bank Rate due to TFSME repayments coinciding with October month-end, Canadian year-end, and US repo spillovers
The Bank's demand-driven repo-led operating framework supplies reserves elastically, but effective market-based finance is also needed for market resilience
why_it_matters: This speech is critical for understanding the structural changes reshaping money markets. As central bank reserves normalize, repo markets face increased demand pressure, creating potential for rate volatility that affects short-term funding costs across the financial system. Market participants trading short-dated rates, repo, or gilts need to understand how these structural shifts may create periodic 'bumps' in money market rates even as policy rates remain stable. The Bank emphasizes its operating framework works as designed during these stress episodes, but the interaction between falling reserves, higher government issuance, and NBFI presence creates a fundamentally different liquidity backdrop than pre-GFC.
market_structure_context: The speech provides detailed analysis of how the Bank of England's operating framework functions within the new liquidity landscape. Key structural elements: (1) STR facility allows unlimited reserve sourcing against Level A collateral (gilts) at Bank Rate; (2) ILTR supplies reserves weekly for six months against broad collateral with minimum spread now 3bps for Level A; (3) The system is demand-driven, meaning reserves supply is determined by counterparties rather than top-down; (4) Combined STR and ILTR supply has grown from £12bn to £152bn in approximately 21 months; (5) Recent repo rate spike to 30bps+ over Bank Rate demonstrates structural friction risk in the transition to PMRR.
important_numbers: £322bn - decrease in sterling reserves from QT and TFSME repayments
£152bn - current reserves supplied by STR and ILTR facilities
£12bn - reserves supplied by facilities in January 2024
£375-540bn - estimated Preferred Minimum Range of Reserves (PMRR)
3 basis points - new minimum spread for Level A collateral in ILTR
30 basis points - recent overnight GC gilt repo rate premium above Bank Rate
0 basis points - previous minimum spread for Level A collateral in ILTR
